question: On the first frosty morning of the year, your tyre pressure warning light comes on, yet none of your tyres has a puncture. What has switched it on?
source_excerpt: why your tire pressure warning light turns on during cold weather

extra.why_interesting: Drivers who see the warning assume a slow puncture. The real cause is ordinary physics they can work out themselves: cold air shrinks. They also learn that the light can switch itself off after a few kilometres.
extra.verification_notes: Cold air contracts and lowers tyre pressure (~1 psi per 10°F), which can trigger the TPMS light without a puncture; this is widely documented (https://clickondetroit.com/automotive/2019/01/31/why-your-tire-pressure-warning-light-turns-on-during-cold-weather).

explanation: Cold air contracts, so tyre pressure drops by roughly 0.1 bar for every 10 °C fall in temperature, which can be enough to trip the sensor. The light often goes off again once driving warms the tyres up, but it's still worth topping them up.

question: One red dashboard warning light looks like a little genie's lamp with a single drop falling from its spout. What object is it really a picture of?
source_excerpt: The oil warning light is usually an oil can icon, often with a drip from the spout, and sometimes labeled "OIL."

extra.why_interesting: Drivers see this lamp-shaped symbol for years without ever wondering what it shows. Most assume it is just an abstract icon or a magic lamp. It is actually a drawing of a tool few modern drivers have ever held, and the drip makes the answer something the player can work out.
extra.verification_notes: The red oil pressure warning light is a standard oil can (oiler) symbol with a drip from the spout; I found no contradicting or newer information, though my sources were low-quality search results.

explanation: It's an old-fashioned oil can, and it means your engine has lost oil pressure. Unlike most lights, this one means pull over and switch off the engine straight away.
